291.quote_or_event: “Speaking what is not commendable–asat–is falsehood (anṛta).” … “What is not laudable? That which causes pain and suffering to the living beings is not commendable. It does not matter whether it refers to the actual fact or not.”
291.explanation: Umāsvāti's definition of falsehood, as explained by Pūjyapāda, rests on harm rather than on factual accuracy. Speech that causes pain to living beings counts as untruth because every Jain vow serves ahiṃsā.
291.tie_back: Valluvar defines truthfulness as speech that harms no one in any way. Pūjyapāda defines its opposite as speech that causes pain to living beings, 'whether it refers to the actual fact or not.' The two definitions mirror each other almost exactly.
291.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.14, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
291._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one match: both define truth by harmlessness rather than by correspondence to fact.

292.quote_or_event: “The mendicant should not tell it, nor show it, he should not comply with their request, but look on silently, or, though knowing it, he should say that he did not know.”
292.explanation: If travellers ask a wandering monk whether he has seen a man or an animal on the road, the Ācārāṅga tells him not to give them away. He should stay silent or, though he knows, say that he does not know, so that no living being comes to harm.
292.tie_back: Valluvar allows that even a falsehood stands in place of truth when it produces faultless good. The Jain monk is likewise permitted to say 'I do not know', against the literal facts, in order to protect life.
292.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.3.3.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 146-147)
292._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a striking concrete case of the Kural's principle, though the text prefers silence first and does not state a general rule that beneficial lies are allowed.

293.quote_or_event: “After and before he has lied, and when he is on the point of lying, he feels infinitely unhappy.”
293.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana describes the inner torment that surrounds a lie: before it, while it is being told, and after it.
293.tie_back: Valluvar warns that once you lie against what your own heart knows, your heart will burn you. The Jain verse likewise places the punishment for lying inside the liar, as 'infinite' unhappiness.
293._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The inner-suffering theme fits well, but Jacobi notes that the Prakrit 'mosa' could also be read as 'stealing', and the verse belongs to a passage about greed for sense-objects.

294.quote_or_event: “A truthful man is treated as reliable as the mother, as venerable as the guru (preceptor) and as beloved as the one who commands knowledge.”
294.explanation: Jain monastic teaching holds that truthfulness earns a person the trust, reverence and affection of everyone around them.
294.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who never lies even in the heart will live in the hearts of all people. The Jain verse says the truthful man becomes trusted like a mother and beloved by all.
294.source: Mūlācāra 837 (Vaṭṭakera), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
294._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com, an English rendering I did not check against the Prakrit. It fits the 'dwelling in all hearts' idea well. A near-identical Saman Suttam rendering of the same idea is used for Kural 97.

295.quote_or_event: “One may have a tuft or matted hair on the head or a shaven head, remain naked or wear a rag. But if he tells a lie, all this is futile or fruitless.”
295.explanation: Śivārya says that all the outward marks of asceticism count for nothing if the ascetic is untruthful. In this text, truth outranks the visible practices of tapas.
295.tie_back: Valluvar ranks the one who speaks truth from the heart above those who practise both austerity and charity. The Jain verse makes the same ranking from the other side: without truth, austerity is fruitless.
295.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 843 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
295._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. It is a strong match on truth outranking austerity, but it does not mention charity (dānam). The verse is also used for Kural 128 in this edition.

296.quote_or_event: “Truthfulness indeed is tapa (penance). In truthfulness do reside self-restraint and all other virtues. Just as the fish can live only in the sea, so can all other virtues reside in Truthfulness alone.”
296.explanation: The Bhagavatī Ārādhanā calls truthfulness the element that all the other virtues live in, as fish live in the sea.
296.tie_back: Valluvar says that never lying brings every other virtue with it, without any strain. The Jain verse says that all virtues live in truthfulness, which is the same claim.
296.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 842 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
296._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. It closely matches 'truth brings all virtues', but has nothing on the Kural's other claim about fame (pugazh).

297.quote_or_event: “Man, understand well the truth! exerting himself in the rule of truth a wise man overcomes Mâra.”
297.explanation: In the Ācārāṅga, Mahāvīra urges the seeker to hold to truth, saying that by exerting himself in truth the wise man overcomes death (Māra). Jainworld renders the same passage as “O Self! Practice Truth, and nothing but Truth.”
297.tie_back: Valluvar says that unbroken truthfulness is enough even without any other virtuous deed. The Ācārāṅga makes the rule of truth by itself sufficient to overcome death.
297.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, p. 33); cf. the Jainworld rendering of the same passage
297._accuracy_note: Jacobi's wording checked on sacred-texts.com, and the Jainworld wording checked separately. The passage puts truth above everything, but it does not say outright, as the Kural does, that other deeds become unnecessary. 'Truth' (sacca) here also carries the sense of doctrinal truth.

298.quote_or_event: “O Brâhmaṇas, why do you tend the fire, and seek external purity by water? The clever ones say that external purity which you seek for, is not the right thing.” … “The Law is my pond, celibacy my holy bathing-place … there I make ablutions; pure, clean, and thoroughly cooled I get rid of hatred (or impurity).”
298.explanation: The low-born monk Harikeśa tells the sacrificing priests that bathing in water gives only outward purity. True cleansing is an inner bath in the Law and in self-restraint, which includes 'abstaining from lying'.
298.tie_back: Valluvar contrasts outer purity from water with inner purity shown through truthfulness. Harikeśa sets the same contrast between washing in water and an inward ethical bath.
298._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The outer/inner purity contrast is exact, but the inner bath is named as the Law and celibacy; truthfulness appears only in the list of restraints at 12.41.

299.quote_or_event: “Enlightened by the light of Truth, the wise transcends death.”
299.explanation: This Jainworld rendering of an Ācārāṅga passage pictures truth as a light that lets the wise go beyond death. The same text calls the great vows, which include truthfulness, a 'light, illumining the three worlds'.
299.tie_back: Valluvar says the lamp of truthfulness is the only real lamp for the wise. The Jain text likewise speaks of 'the light of Truth' as what truly illuminates the wise.
299.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3 (Jainworld cites 3/3/66), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'; cf. Ācārāṅga II.16.6 (tr. Jacobi, SBE 22)
299._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. The light image is a free rendering: Jacobi's translation of the same passage has no lamp or light, and 'truth' there means doctrinal truth more than truthful speech.

300.quote_or_event: “Truth alone is the essence in the world.”
300.explanation: The Praśnavyākaraṇa, a Śvetāmbara Aṅga that sets out the five vows, praises truth as the very essence of the world.
300.tie_back: Valluvar ends the chapter by saying that among all the real things he has found, none is better than truthfulness. The Jain Aṅga makes the same supreme claim: truth alone is the essence of the world.
300.source: Praśnavyākaraṇa Sūtra 2.2, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
300._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. I did not check it against a scholarly translation of the Praśnavyākaraṇa, but as a supreme valuation of truth it matches the Kural very closely.
